query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys, systematic variation of Al content controls the formation of B2-type (or short-range ordered) domains, which stabilize the microstructure under extreme conditions and enhance strength, environmental resistance, and radiation tolerance without severely degrading cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline near-equiatomic Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with minimal or zero Al content, exhibiting a primarily single-phase FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Incrementally increase Al content (e.g., from 0 to ~8–10 at.%) in a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni samples.
generation.conditions: Perform XRD and electron microscopy under a range of temperatures (cryogenic to ~800 °C), including controlled radiation exposure and oxidative environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The fraction and spatial distribution of B2-ordered domains or short-range ordering around Al sites in the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Al-driven ordering reduces interfacial energy and enhances defect absorption, leading to B2-stabilized regions that improve mechanical strength (by impeding dislocation motion) and radiation resistance, while retaining adequate ductility and toughness at low temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples containing intermediate levels of Al will exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength (on the order of hundreds of MPa) and improved radiation damage tolerance compared to the baseline, with only moderate reductions in cryogenic toughness. Excess Al, however, may promote excessively brittle oxides or extensive second-phase formation with detrimental effects on ductility.
generation.baseline: An Al-free Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy showing good ductility and toughness but relatively lower strength and decreased resistance to radiation damage compared to Al-bearing compositions.
generation.boundary: For significantly higher Al contents than tested here or changes to the other principal elements (e.g., substituting elements beyond Co–Cr–Fe–Ni), the hypothesized B2-stabilizing effect and property enhancements may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: Exact compositional thresholds and domain sizes governing the transition from beneficial to detrimental influences remain underexplored and may be environment- and processing-dependent.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy batches with Al contents ranging from 0 to 10 at%. Characterize the microstructure (via XRD, SEM/TEM), mechanical behavior (yield strength, ductility, fracture toughness), and radiation tolerance (microstructure after irradiation). Compare results systematically across the Al concentration series.
measurements: Fraction and size of B2 domains (TEM)
Yield and tensile strengths, ductility (mechanical testing)
Radiation damage observation (TEM of irradiated samples)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing Al content does not correlate with B2 domain formation or short-range ordering and does not improve high-temperature and radiation performance above the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys have good application prospects in nuclear power plants due to their excellent mechanical properties and radiation resistance. In this paper, the microstructure of the Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 high-entropy alloy was researched using metallurgical microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy. The mechanical properties were tested using a Vickers microhardness tester and a tensile testing machine, respectively. The results showed that Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 had a single-phase, disordered, face-centered, cubic solid-solution structure and was strengthened by solid solution. The alloy lattice parameter and density were estimated as 0.304 nm and 7.89 g/cm3, respectively. The test results indicated that the alloy had satisfactory mechanical properties with yield stress and tensile strength of about 530 MPa and 985 MPa, respectively.

High-entropy alloys are composed of a minimum of five components, whose concentrations are approximately between 5 and 35 at.%. HEAs show some distinct features, for example, excellent mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, and high temperature oxidation properties. Since the high-entropy alloys may have various outstanding properties, they are of considerable importance in engineering applications [,,]. In the study of the HEAs containing aluminum by transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations, phase transformations—such as precipitation transformation [,,], spinodal decomposition [,,,,], and ordering reaction [,]—were found, and their product phases were L12 [,,], and B2 [,,,,,] superlattices.
